## Purpose

This SOP describes standardized procedures for recording geographic
coordinates, navigating to field sites, and managing waypoint data.
Accurate and consistent location data are essential for linking field
observations to spatial analyses, returning to the same sampling points
across seasons, and sharing site information among researchers. This
SOP covers handheld GPS receivers, smartphone GPS applications, and
post-field data management [@usfs_gps2012].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities that require
  geographic coordinates, including sample collection, transect
  establishment, monitoring well location, equipment installation, and
  site reconnaissance
- **Does not apply to:** High-precision survey-grade GNSS work
  (sub-centimeter accuracy); drone-based georeferencing (see
  [SOP-F630](SOP-F630-drone-operations.qmd)); GIS post-processing and
  spatial analysis (see future SOP-L804)
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve coordinate system and datum for each project    |
| Trained Personnel | Record waypoints per this SOP, upload data after fieldwork |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## Definitions

- **Datum:** A mathematical model of the Earth's surface used as the
  reference for geographic coordinates; the EA Program default is
  **WGS 84** (World Geodetic System 1984), the datum used by
  consumer GPS and Google Maps; NAD 83 is nearly identical for most
  field purposes but must be specified explicitly if used
  [@usfs_gps2012].
- **Decimal degrees (DD):** A coordinate format expressing latitude
  and longitude as a single decimal number (e.g., 34.0975 N,
  117.7125 W); the EA Program default format; preferred for data entry
  in spreadsheets and GIS.
- **GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System):** The general term for
  satellite-based positioning systems; includes the US GPS, Russian
  GLONASS, European Galileo, and Chinese BeiDou constellations; modern
  receivers use multiple constellations simultaneously to improve
  accuracy.
- **GPS (Global Positioning System):** The US-operated GNSS
  constellation of 31+ satellites; provides horizontal accuracy of
  3--5 m under open sky with a modern consumer receiver [@usfs_gps2012].
- **GPX file:** A standard XML-based file format for exchanging GPS
  waypoints, tracks, and routes between devices and software;
  the preferred export format for EA Program waypoints.
- **HDOP (Horizontal Dilution of Precision):** A dimensionless number
  indicating GPS positional uncertainty due to satellite geometry;
  values below 2 indicate excellent geometry; values above 5 indicate
  poor geometry and reduced accuracy [@usfs_gps2012].
- **Offline map:** A map tile set downloaded to a smartphone or
  device before the field visit, enabling navigation without cellular
  data; required for EA Program field sites with unreliable coverage.
- **UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator):** A projected coordinate
  system that divides the world into 60 zones and expresses positions
  in meters east (easting) and north (northing) of a zone origin;
  useful for measuring distances directly but requires specifying the
  UTM zone.
- **Waypoint:** A named, saved geographic location stored in a GPS
  receiver or smartphone app; defined by coordinates (latitude,
  longitude, and optionally elevation), a name, and often a
  description or icon.
- **WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984):** The global coordinate
  datum used by GPS satellites, Google Maps, and most modern
  consumer GPS devices; the EA Program default [@usfs_gps2012].


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Navigating to remote waypoints may involve uneven
  terrain, dense vegetation, or stream crossings. Do not fixate on
  the GPS screen while walking.
- **Environmental:** Reliance on GPS in areas with poor satellite
  coverage (dense canopy, steep canyons) can lead to navigation
  errors. Always carry a paper map or site sketch as a backup.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). If lost or
disoriented, stop moving, note your last known coordinates, and contact
the field lead by phone or walkie-talkie.


## Equipment and Materials

| Item                                      | Notes                                    |
|:------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Handheld GPS receiver (Garmin or equivalent) | Check battery level; carry spare batteries [@garmin_gpsmap66] |
| Smartphone with GPS app                   | Avenza Maps, Gaia GPS, or similar app with offline map capability [@avenza_guide] |
| Backup paper map or site sketch           | Annotated with known landmarks and access roads |
| Field notebook                            | For recording waypoint IDs and descriptions |
| USB cable or Bluetooth adapter            | For downloading waypoints to a computer  |
| Spare batteries (AA or rechargeable)      | Matched to the GPS unit model            |


## Procedure

### Pre-Field Setup

1. Confirm the coordinate system and datum for the project. The EA
   Program default is **WGS 84, latitude/longitude in decimal degrees**
   [@usfs_gps2012]. If a project requires UTM or NAD 83, configure the
   device accordingly and note the setting in the field notebook.
2. On a handheld GPS, verify the datum setting: navigate to
   Setup > Position Format and confirm WGS 84 [@garmin_gpsmap66].
3. On a smartphone app, enable offline maps for the study area. Do
   not rely on cellular data for map tiles in the field [@avenza_guide].
4. Clear or archive old waypoints from the device so the day's data
   are easy to identify.
5. Pre-load target waypoints if revisiting known sites. Use the naming
   convention described in §6.3.

### Recording Waypoints in the Field

1. At the sampling location, hold the GPS receiver at chest height in
   an open area away from dense canopy, cliff faces, and vehicles.
2. Wait until the GPS reports an accuracy of 5 m or better (HDOP < 2
   preferred). If accuracy remains above 5 m after two minutes, record
   the waypoint and note the reported accuracy in the field notebook
   [@usfs_gps2012].
3. Save the waypoint using the naming convention in §6.3.
4. In the field notebook, record:
   - Waypoint name
   - Date and time
   - Coordinates (as displayed on the device)
   - Reported accuracy (HDOP or meters, as available)
   - A brief description (e.g., "upstream riffle, transect 3 start")
5. If using a smartphone, take a screenshot of the GPS display as a
   backup record.

### Waypoint Naming Convention

Use the following format: `SITE_TYPE_NN`

- `SITE` = three- or four-letter site abbreviation (e.g., BFS, THW, MRW)
- `TYPE` = two-letter code for the point type (see table below)
- `NN` = sequential two-digit number

| Code | Point Type                | Example     |
|:-----|:--------------------------|:------------|
| WQ   | Water quality sampling    | BFS_WQ_01   |
| SO   | Soil sampling             | THW_SO_03   |
| TR   | Transect endpoint         | MRW_TR_01   |
| WL   | Monitoring well           | BFS_WL_02   |
| RF   | Reference / benchmark     | THW_RF_01   |
| GN   | General / other           | MRW_GN_05   |

If a project requires a different convention, document it in the
project README and field notebook.

### Navigating to Existing Waypoints

1. Load the target waypoint on the GPS receiver or smartphone app.
2. Use the "Navigate" or "Go To" function. Follow the bearing
   indicator, checking your surroundings periodically.
3. When the GPS indicates you are within the reported accuracy of the
   waypoint, look for physical markers (flagging, rebar, painted rocks)
   to confirm the exact location.
4. If the physical marker cannot be found, record a new waypoint at
   the location you judge to be correct and note the discrepancy in
   the field notebook.

### Post-Field Data Management

1. Download waypoints from the GPS receiver to the project computer
   within 48 hours of returning from the field.
2. Export waypoints as a `.gpx` or `.csv` file and save to the project
   GitHub repository under `data/gps/`.
3. Use the file naming convention: `YYYY-MM-DD_SiteID_waypoints.gpx`
4. Verify that waypoint names match the field notebook entries.
   Correct any discrepancies before committing the file.
5. Back up the raw GPS file to the lab shared drive.


## Quality Control

- Compare GPS coordinates against known benchmarks or previously
  recorded waypoints when revisiting sites. Discrepancies greater than
  10 m should be investigated and noted [@usfs_gps2012].
- At least once per semester, verify the GPS receiver against a known
  benchmark (e.g., a USGS survey marker or campus reference point).
- Record the GPS model, serial number, and firmware version in the
  field notebook at the start of each project.

## Training Record

Before using GPS equipment independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate proper waypoint recording (datum check, accuracy
   verification, naming convention) during a supervised field visit
3. Successfully download and export waypoints to the project repository
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
